narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Sundanese dances developed largely among common people in the mountain villages of Priangan and Banten, driven by the absence of a centralized court culture (keraton) following the fall of the Sunda Pajajaran kingdom in the late 16th century.
In the 17th century, the Priangan region was held under the Javanese Mataram kingdom for 50 years, introducing Javanese cultural influences like wayang and dance styles.
on_screen: Map: Indonesia · Southeast Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Integrates ritual, artistic expression, entertainment, and social conduct.
At weddings and village ceremonies, men dance enthusiastically to drum beats.
Henry Spiller's research notes that men use dance to explore gender identities through a triangle of female entertainers, drumming, and freedom.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Referred to as ngibing, Sundanese dance is typically performed between male and female couples with cheerful, dynamic, and expressive flowing movements that sync with the kendang beat.
Popular styles include Jaipongan (solo, group, or couple formats), Merak (peafowl mimicry), and dances incorporating Pencak Silat martial arts movements or comical Reog routines.
Watch for Merak peafowl mimicry, Ngibing social dance.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Performed at village ceremonies, weddings, and harvest festivals like Seren Taun in mountainous Priangan rice farming villages, as well as on stages. Costumes include peafowl-inspired attire for the Merak dance and traditional regional garments.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Integrates ritual, artistic expression, entertainment, and social conduct. At weddings and village ceremonies, men dance enthusiastically to drum beats. Henry Spiller's research notes that men use dance to explore gender identities through a triangle of female entertainers, drumming, and freedom. Dances like Buyung celebrate the Seren Taun rice harvest.
